# Question

**What percent of college professors consider themselves "above-average" teachers?** Cross (1977, "Not can, but will: college teaching") reported faculty self-ratings across U.S. colleges.

## Data source

Reconstructed counts (n = 250) calibrated to the published 94% headline figure; the original per-institution breakdown is not available.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Self-rated above-average vs the statistical ceiling"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
ax.bar(["Self-rated above\naverage", "Statistically\npossible"], [0.94, 0.50],
       color=["#c76c6c", "#999999"])
ax.axhline(0.5, ls="--", color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("Proportion")
for x, v in enumerate([0.94, 0.50]):
    ax.text(x, v + 0.02, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

One-proportion z vs H₀: p = 0.5, exact binomial, 100k-replicate randomization, and Wald + bootstrap CIs.

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| Point estimate | p̂ = **94%** above average (235 / 250) |
| 95% CI (Wald / bootstrap) | (91.1%, 96.9%) / (90.8%, 96.8%) |
| z vs 50% | z = 13.9, p ≈ 5e-44 |
| Exact binomial (two-sided) | p ≈ 5e-52 |
| Randomization (100k) | p < 1e-5 |

# Decision

Statistically **impossible** for 94% to be above average — at most ~50% plus sampling noise can exceed the median. A textbook better-than-average effect (illusory superiority), rivalling the famous 93% of drivers who rate themselves above average.
